The direction matters more than the destination at the moment but a few crossroads approach
On 11/8 We publish "Clear Sailing" calling for a growth scare.  Red Star.  We even called for the crazy ivan rip to 7650 Green Dotted line.  Now we are back on the growth scare path in which very short stocks and moderately long bonds is the trade.  
That path could V bottom or head to recession island.  
First fork in the road is the orange dotted line in which the private economy is strong enough to reverse the growth scare.  
If it fails the growth scare becomes a growth slowdown Purple Dotted line.  
If that fails the growth slowdown reaches another fork.  The Red line is the recessionista favorite.  Stocks go down less fast but bond yields collapse. 
At that fork the policymakers intervene eventually. when they do the light blue line is the move.  We think its closer to 6000 before intervention can kick in.  
The key takeaway is the current path positioning isnt much different until the fork in the road.

tweets.text:
Experiments are everything.

No experiments = no growth; so I always spend a % of my income to test new growth ideas.

6 lessons from my Oct–Nov experiments ↓

1. Keep important links in standalone X posts

→ Standalone posts with links: 1.16% conversion
→ Links as comments (part of thread): 0.07% conversion

Standalone posts also brought 7–17 website visits, compared to just 1–2 from threads.

2. Influencer ads are expensive even if horizontal

In Oct, I started sponsoring recommendations and mentions on Substack to promote my newsletter.

→ Spent: $2,258
→ Acquired: 40 subscribers
→ Cost per subscriber: $56

But: Recommendations are 3 months min – so the cost per subscriber keeps declining with time – but it's still very far from $10-$15 many teams expect from creators.

Overall, paid recommendations from smaller newsletters performed better than sponsored mentions.

3. Compare subscriber engagement by source

Email open rates varied considerably by cohorts; depending on where they came from:

→ Substack recommendations: 19%
→ X: 42%

So not all followers are "equal".

4. Prioritize practical content

My zero-budget marketing guide generated 893 views and 16 subscribers.

A typical newsletter issue gets 170–340 views and 1–5 subscribers.

So I'll be focusing more on practical guides from now on.

5. Find hidden Telegram traffic

Telegram sent readers to my newsletter, but those visits appeared as "direct" traffic.

Now I add UTM tags to every link I share there, so I can see exactly how much traffic comes from Telegram in my analytics.

6. Don't trust gut feeling when posting

Posts I expected to perform well were often average, while some random ones did surprisingly well.

Even after years of creating content, it's almost impossible to predict how posts will perform.

Anyway, this period gave me quite a few reasons to rethink how I promote @StacysBrain.

Very productive and insightful 6 weeks :)

PS: I have a guide on how I set up my analytics system; you can read it here ↓

https://newsletter.stacysbrain.com/p/cross-channel-analytics

PPS: Don't forget to subscribe <3

$P earnings were actually interesting, not really in terms actionable investments. 

But more on AI capex broadening, where deployments are happening, and what Jensen at $NVDA might envisioned with open weight model + GPU demand. 

- Everpure CEO stated that enterprises are increasingly building on-premises AI factories, stating: 

"The ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront."

- "I'm talking about standard enterprises, regular finance organizations. A wide variety of organizations are starting to buy these AI factories for the purpose of running their own open weight models

From "regular insurance companies, et cetera"

- "One is they're starting to see that these open weight models are actually being able to provide good results, and they're doing so at a fraction of the cost of using the cloud for these workloads"

"that the ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront"

This type of broad industry transition would be heavily bearish as it threatens $ANT, OpenAI and frontier labs over the long term... 

And probably what Jensen saw things heading with $NVDA + additional GPU demand regardless of what frontier lab wins. 

However, I expect more of the open weight effort to collapse or see heavier regulation with how Washington + frontier labs were lobbying. 

- In regards to NAND prices dropping: "If prices come down slowly, I expect to see demand come up along with that" (Jevon) 

- LOL this part was hilarious and the same argument I was using for why qualification cycle players like in optics were so interesting. 

On data center slowdown potential:

"So on the first part of it, remember, I mean, really, the thing that insulates us is we have such a small share going into the hyperscale market"

"even in a down market, they’re going to spend a lot more than our current share amounts to", and their market capture goes up over time relative to overall TAM.

Markets appear to be wrongly interpreting Chinese eSSD cuts as deteriorating demand and NAND oversupply.

Phison CEO commentary today + more context behind $SNDK / Kioxia selloff regarding Trendforce revisions: 

- "Pua attributed China's recent enterprise SSD demand slowdown to GPU shortages since November 2026"

- "Without GPUs, additional purchases offer little value, prompting some companies to sell server components on the spot market to recover cash" 

(for context enterprise SSDs are growth driver for NAND)

- "Chinese cloud giants nevertheless plan substantial GPU prepayments, temporarily tying up capital and delaying procurement of other components."

- "the principal challenge in 2027 would be insufficient supply rather than weakening demand, with persistent AI shortages potentially prompting further procurement and inventory accumulation."

Markets seemed to have wrongly interpreted this as demand destruction + pricing collapse. 

When Phison CEO attributed it to 
-> GPU shortages 
-> causing procurement timing mismatch 
-> Chinese CSPs needed capital for GPU prepayments, so liquidation in inventory (causing spot price volatility)
-> timeline shift in order procurement 

TLDR: delayed procurement from GPU shortages. there were actual order cuts, but this is deferred procurement not structural demand weakening. 

Chinese CSPs needed capital for GPU prepayments so they liquidated other inventories in the meantime. 

Phison says its inventories are insufficient for anticipated 2027 demand and it's sees this as an opportunity for NAND accumulation. 

It's interesting the bottleneck in China migrated back to GPUs though.

Supply procurement is accelerating... from $SOI selling $1.2B in agreements, in a single quarter (from $25M revenue/quarter). To $COHR signing $20B in LTAs, to $LITE selling out of 2029 capacity.

Even if you stress test aggregate capex slowdown or accelerator flood vs. grid constraint/permitting downside:

- There's an economic incentive to improve GPU efficiency and power utilization. (eg. Lambda's CPO data suggests enough power savings to support ~4.5% more GPUs)... for power constrained DCs. 

- There's an economic incentive to reduce expensive HBM4 requirements in certain cases (eg. $MRVL estimating up to 30% savings through optical memory pooling)... for memory constrained inference. 

While for economic upside in these companies:

-> Optical networking, and their upstream materials like substrates and lasers represent a relatively small fraction of total AI cluster BOM.

-> At the same time, optical content goes up...while selling prices of that content rise nonlinearly as well (lasers 10x+ selling price from pluggable to CPO.)

- Many low end players eg. 400G/800G, module assemblers etc. don't capture the same scale in economics from the NPO/CPO transitions... compared to laser suppliers, fiber array suppliers, modulator suppliers, or companies in the ELS/optical engine stacks.

US consumer sentiment and inflation expectations, further Fed commentary, and whether the dollar finally loses momentum.

Crypto feels dead right now.

But in 2021, blockchains took 62% of crypto fees. Today, apps take over 95%.

Need some hopium?

Here are 4 areas of crypto still making real progress:

1. Tokens that buy themselves back

For years, the whole plan for most tokens was "buy it and hope someone else pays more later." Not exactly a business model.

Now Hyperliquid, Uniswap and pump .fun use their revenue to buy back or burn their own tokens. Hyperliquid especially, since it makes serious money from real trading.

That means usage can create demand for the token even when nobody's in the mood to buy. Basically, the protocol is the one buyer that never panic sells.

Unlocks still matter, so check that the buybacks are bigger than the new supply hitting the market.

2. Private AI is becoming a real business

Privacy has become one of the more interesting sectors this cycle, and Zcash is getting a lot of renewed interest.

The one I'm watching most closely is Venice. It sells private AI access and uses part of what people pay to buy back and burn $VVV.

New tokens are still being created faster than they're burned, though, so I'm watching it rather than buying it yet.

3. Wall Street is still moving onchain

About $39B of real-world assets, not counting stablecoins, are already tokenized.

Even with everyone scared, BlackRock and other big firms keep bringing traditional financial products onto blockchain rails. They're not checking the Fear & Greed Index every morning like the rest of us. They're planning for years, not weeks.

4. Stablecoins don't need a bull market

There's about $284B in stablecoins today, and more companies are using them to send money across borders.

Tether, Circle and Stripe are all building around this.

A business paying someone overseas doesn't care what BTC did this week. It just wants the money to arrive faster and cheaper, without a bank calling it "3 to 5 business days."

What I'm doing with this

The Fear & Greed Index is at 12, while these businesses keep building.

I'm lining up projects from these four areas and looking for ones where revenue is growing while the price keeps falling. That's the setup I want to be early on when sentiment flips.

I don't know if that's next month or next year, and plenty of tokens won't make it back. But the businesses are still running.

What part of crypto gives you the most conviction right now?

“Ben Graham, my friend and teacher, long ago described the mental attitude toward market fluctuations that I believe to be most conducive to investment success. He said that you should imagine market quotations as coming from a remarkably accommodating fellow named Mr. Market who is your partner in a private business. Without fail, Mr. Market appears daily and names a price at which he will either buy your interest or sell you his. 

Even though the business that the two of you own may have economic characteristics that are stable, Mr. Market's quotations will be anything but. For, sad to say, the poor fellow has incurable emotional problems. At times he feels euphoric and can see only the favorable factors affecting the business. When in that mood, he names a very high buy-sell price because he fears that you will snap up his interest and rob him of imminent gains. At other times he is depressed and can see nothing but trouble ahead for both the business and the world. On these occasions he will name a very low price, since he is terrified that you will unload your interest on him.

Mr. Market has another endearing characteristic: He doesn't mind being ignored. If his quotation is uninteresting to you today, he will be back with a new one tomorrow. Transactions are strictly at your option.

Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you."

- Warren Buffet (1987 Shareholder Letter)

At this stage, its not conclusive that we are in a lengthy bear-market. Even those bear-markets had face ripping multi-week rallies and in terms of positioning and sentiment we are very washed out now.

The TMT bust (2000-2002) was triggered by tight monetary which inverted the yield curve and caused a recession. Back then, the NASDAQ also traded at an absurd valuation. Today, the yield curve is not inverted and the NASDAQ's forward PE is at the same level as the COVID-crash low!

The 2008 bust was triggered by the housing bubble and the collapse of various banks; which is not the case today. 

The 2022 bear market was triggered by the Federal Reserve which abruptly ended massive QE and embarked on a severe rate hiking cycle. This is also not similar with the current situation. 

This time around, the market is worrying about a slowdown in AI capex for 2028 and beyond; and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership and circular financing arrangements. In spring the market was also very worried about AI killing cybersecurity and infrastructure software companies and that turned out to be dead wrong. 

The jury is still out on how the Dems sweep will impact the AI capex cycle and how Nvidia's next CEO will manage the business. During times like these when most are super bearish and sentiment is super negative, best to remain calm and focus on the facts.
